claim: The guenons are a group of African primates consisting of 25–38 recognized species.

claim: The objectivity of the occlude-reclassify approach is important because it allows researchers to intelligently target specific signal components for further analysis without reference to their own perceptions of their salience.
source: The objectivity of the approach is important, as it allows researchers to intelligently targetspecific signal components for further analysis without reference to their own perceptions of their salience.
evidence: The claim is based on inference about the advantages of the method.

claim: The objectivity of the occlude-reclassify approach is particularly important when studying species with sensory and perceptual systems very different from our own.
source: This is particularly important when studying species with sensory and perceptual systems very different from our own (Endler, 1990; Bennett et al., 1994).
evidence: The claim is based on inference and citations to work on sensory ecology.

claim: Combining the occlude-reclassify approach with a biologically realistic encoding scheme increases the biological validity of results.
source: Where possible, combining this approach with a biologically realistic encoding scheme, such as classification within a perceptual face space based on eigenface scores (Leopold et al., 2001; Cowen et al., 2014; Chang and Tsao, 2017) as used here, increases the biological validity of results.
evidence: The claim is based on inference about methodological best practices, supported by citations.

claim: Guenon behavioral repertoires, such as nose-to-nose touching, reflect the importance and biological relevance of facial traits.
source: Guenon behavioral repertoires, such as nose-to-nose touching observed in wild putty nosed monkeys (SW, personal observation) and red-tailed monkeys (Estes, 1991), further reflect the importance and biological relevance of these traits.
evidence: The claim is based on observational data and citation to published observations.

claim: Primates preferentially attend to facial information.
source: Primates preferentially attend to facial information (Tsao et al., 2008; Kano and Tomonaga, 2009)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to neuroscience and behavioral studies.

claim: Face patterns are particularly suited to influencing behavior and decision-making in con- and heterospecifics.
source: making face patterns particularly suited to influencing behavior and decision-making in con- and heterospecifics.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the fact that primates attend to faces.

claim: Multiple other primate groups are characterized by rapid speciation, high degrees of sympatry, and diverse facial appearances.
source: Interestingly, multiple other primate groups are also characterized by rapid speciation, high degrees of sympatry, and diverse facial appearances (e.g. callitrichids, Opazo et al., 2006; gibbons, Carbone et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies of other primate groups.

claim: Comparative analyses have linked face pattern complexity to number of sympatric congenerics in primates.
source: and comparative analyses have linked face pattern complexity to number of sympatric congenerics in primates (Santana et al., 2012; Santana et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to comparative studies.

claim: Selection for species discrimination may be a key driver of diversity in primates.
source: suggesting that selection for species discrimination may be a key driver of diversity in this group.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from comparative analyses cited.

claim: The work links signal appearance to visual attention in a recent and diverse primate radiation.
source: Our work linking signal appearance to visual attention in a recent and diverse primate radiation
evidence: The claim summarizes the contribution of the current study.

claim: Evolutionary processes involving species discrimination can be important in generating animal phenotypes.
source: highlights how such evolutionary processes can be important in generating animal phenotypes.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the study's findings about the broader implications.

claim: The analysis is based on 599 total images of 133 individuals, collectively representing 15 guenon species.
source: Our analysis is therefore based on 599 total images of 133 individuals, collectively representing 15 guenon species (for species-specific sample sizes, see Figure 2).
evidence: The claim describes the dataset used in the study.

claim: All correctly classified images (n = 654) were used to identify face regions of critical importance to correct species classification.
source: All correctly classified images (n = 654) were used to identify face regions of critical importance to correct species classification by the computer algorithm, using our occlude-reclassify scheme.
evidence: The claim describes the methodology and sample used.

claim: Looking time experiments were conducted at CERCOPAN sanctuary in Calabar, Nigeria.
source: Looking time experiments were conducted at CERCOPAN sanctuary in Calabar, Nigeria
evidence: The claim describes the location of the experimental work.

claim: The experiments included 18 adult putty nosed monkeys.
source: and included 18 adult putty nosed monkeys (C. nictitans; n males = 6, n females = 12; mean (range) age = 13 (7-22) years)
evidence: The claim describes the experimental subjects.

claim: The experiments included 16 adult mona monkeys.
source: and 16 adult mona monkeys (C. mona; n males = 10, n females = 6; mean (range) age = 8.8 (3–24) years).
evidence: The claim describes the experimental subjects.

claim: All subjects were socially housed with other guenons in groups of two to five.
source: and were socially housed with other guenons in groups of two to five (mean = 4).
evidence: The claim describes the housing conditions of experimental subjects.

claim: All subjects were within visual range of heterospecific guenon species.
source: All subjects were within visual range of heterospecific guenon species, which included C. erythrotis, C. mona, C. nictitians, C. preussi, C. sclateri, Ch. tantalus, and E. patas
evidence: The claim describes the visual environment of experimental subjects.

claim: Reliability was assessed using approximately 10% of all trial videos, with agreement between two coders on the direction of jointly coded looks within these trials being in agreement in 94.46% of frames.
source: Reliability was assessed using approximately 10% of all trial videos, in which we assessed agreement between two coders on the direction of jointly coded looks within these trials as being in agreement in 94.46% of frames (Cohen's kappa = 0.883)
evidence: The claim describes the reliability assessment of video coding.

claim: The reliability score is well within the range of acceptable reliability scores for this type of data.
source: which is well within the range of acceptable reliability scores for this type of data (Winters et al., 2015; Dubuc et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to methodological standards.

claim: The nose spot of the putty nosed monkey was the most critical facial feature identified across all species.
source: For example, the nose spot of the putty nosed monkey was the most critical facial feature identified across all species.
evidence: The claim is supported by the computational analysis results.

claim: Results generated using subsets of species that have range overlap with putty nosed monkeys and mona monkeys were similar to those generated using the entire image set.
source: Results generated using subsets of species that have range overlap with putty nosed monkeys and mona monkeys were similar to those generated using the entire image set.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of results from different analyses.

claim: The critical facial regions identified when comparing the putty nosed monkey with sympatric species also included the nose spot as the only essential feature.
source: In particular, the critical facial regions identified when comparing the putty nosed monkey with sympatric species also included the nose spot as the only essential feature (Figure 2—figure supplements 4–7).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Analyses run on left and right hemi-faces differed somewhat in how important different face regions were for correct classification of mona monkeys.
source: Analyses run on left and right hemi-faces differed somewhat in how important different face regions were for correct classification, but taken as a whole still show that a broader face region including eyebrow patches is important for correct classification when classifying mona monkeys with respect to sympatric species (Figure 2—figure supplements 8–11).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in supplementary figures.
